blocks.text: Vulval cancer is a malignant tumour arising from the external female genitalia, including the labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule and other vulval structures.
A. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)

blocks.title: The most common type. It often develops through one of two pathways:

items.text: HPV-associated disease, often linked to high-risk HPV types.
HPV-independent disease, frequently associated with chronic vulval dermatoses such as lichen sclerosus and with TP53 abnormalities.

blocks.text: B. Vulval melanoma
A less common but potentially aggressive malignancy. It may appear as a changing pigmented lesion, although not all melanomas are darkly pigmented.
C. Other rare cancers
These include Bartholin gland carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, basal cell carcinoma and sarcomas.
VIN is a pre-invasive abnormality of the vulval epithelium. It is not the same as invasive vulval cancer.

items.text: Vulvar high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (vHSIL): usually HPV-associated.
Differentiated VIN (dVIN): usually HPV-independent and often associated with lichen sclerosus; it carries a significant risk of progression to invasive SCC.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Do not confuse VIN with invasive cancer. Histology determines whether invasion is present.

blocks.text: Vulval lymphatic drainage commonly passes to the superficial and deep inguinal nodes, then to pelvic nodes. Nodal involvement is an important determinant of prognosis and adjuvant treatment.

blocks.text: Lichen sclerosus is associated with HPV-independent vulval SCC. Treatment commonly includes an ultrapotent topical corticosteroid, such as clobetasol propionate, under appropriate clinical guidance.

Patients need education about regular use, follow-up and reporting new focal thickening, ulceration or a persistent lesion. Treating lichen sclerosus reduces symptoms and inflammation but does not eliminate the need to investigate suspicious changes.
Prognosis depends on stage, tumour size, depth of invasion, nodal involvement, histology and response to treatment.

blocks.text: Follow-up includes examination of the vulva and groins, surveillance for recurrence and management of treatment effects. Patients should know to report a new lesion, ulcer, lump, persistent itching or groin swelling.

subsections.subsection_title: 12. Counselling a patient with suspected vulval cancer

blocks.text: A counselling station assesses empathy, explanation of uncertainty and shared decision-making.

items.text: Ask what the patient understands about the lesion.
Explain why its appearance or persistence requires further investigation.
Explain the purpose of biopsy and how it is performed.
Clarify that a suspicious lesion does not automatically mean cancer.
Discuss what happens if the biopsy confirms malignancy.
Explore concerns about surgery, sexual function, urinary function, body image and lymphoedema.
Explain the role of the specialist team and the importance of follow-up.
Offer psychological support and invite questions.

blocks.text: “I understand that finding a persistent lesion in this area can be worrying and may feel difficult to discuss. There are several possible causes, including inflammatory skin conditions and precancerous changes, but we need to exclude cancer. The most reliable way to do that is to take a small sample for examination under a microscope. Once we have the result, we can discuss the appropriate treatment and any effects it may have on your comfort, sexual function and everyday life.”

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the most common histological type of vulval cancer?
Squamous cell carcinoma.
Q2. What are the two major pathways to vulval SCC?
HPV-associated disease, often preceded by vulval HSIL, and HPV-independent disease, often associated with lichen sclerosus and differentiated VIN.
Q3. What is the most important investigation for a suspicious vulval lesion?
A properly obtained vulval biopsy for histopathology.
Q4. What are the important prognostic factors?
Tumour stage, size, depth of invasion, regional lymph-node involvement, histological characteristics and recurrence status.
Q5. Why examine the groins?
The inguinal lymph nodes are major regional drainage sites for the vulva, and nodal metastasis affects staging, prognosis and treatment.
Q6. What is the role of sentinel lymph node biopsy?
It can assess regional nodal involvement while reducing morbidity compared with full groin lymph-node dissection in appropriately selected early-stage cases.
Q7. What is differentiated VIN?
An HPV-independent pre-invasive lesion, often associated with lichen sclerosus, that has a meaningful risk of progression to invasive SCC and generally warrants excision.
Q8. Does a negative HPV test exclude vulval cancer?
No. HPV-independent vulval cancer occurs, and diagnosis depends on clinical assessment and histology.
Q9. What complications may follow inguinofemoral lymphadenectomy?
Wound infection, lymphocele, wound breakdown and lower-limb or vulval lymphoedema.
Q10. How should persistent itching in an older woman be managed?

Take a focused history, examine the vulva carefully, assess for dermatoses and suspicious lesions, and arrange biopsy or specialist assessment when indicated rather than repeatedly prescribing empirical treatment.
